ENGINEERING
Coding Standards
Language style, naming, branching, code review, testing and security rules for all Nexora repositories
Document ID
NX-ENG-003
Version
2.6
Document
owner
Engineering Excellence Guild
Effective date
1 February 2026
Applies to
All engineers and contractors
contributing to Nexora repositories
Classification
Internal - Confidential
Abstract. This document sets the mandatory coding standards for Nexora Technologies. It defines language versions and
tooling for Python and TypeScript, naming conventions, the Git branching model, commit message format, pull request and
code review rules, minimum test coverage by module tier, logging practices and security requirements. The aim is
consistent, readable and safe code that any engineer can review and maintain.
Keywords: coding standards, Python, TypeScript, PEP 8, Git branching, code review, unit testing, secrets management

Formatters and linters run as pre-commit hooks and again in CI; formatting comments in reviews are therefore
discouraged. Python dependencies are pinned in requirements.txt or pyproject.toml with a lock file.

# Not acceptable # Preferred
def proc(d): def route_ticket(ticket: Ticket, rules: list[Rule]) -> Queue:
 for r in rules: """Return the queue whose rule first matches the ticket."""
 if r(d): return r.q for rule in rules:
 if rule.matches(ticket):
 return rule.queue
 raise NoMatchingRuleError(ticket.id)
3. Git Branching Model
Nexora uses a simplified GitFlow model (Figure 1). The main branch always mirrors production and is
protected; direct pushes are not allowed. Engineers create feature/* branches from develop, open a pull
request, and merge after review. Release branches stabilise a version, and urgent production fixes use
hotfix/* branches that are merged to both main and develop.
Figure 1. Branching model: main, develop, feature, release and hotfix branches.
3.1 Commit Messages
Commits follow the Conventional Commits format: type(scope): summary, using the types feat, fix,
docs, refactor, test and chore. The summary is at most 72 characters and written in the imperative mood,
for example fix(tickets): prevent duplicate creation on retry.
4. Code Review Rules
Table 3. Pull request and review requirements.
Rule
Requirement
Reviewers
At least 1 approval; 2 approvals for changes to authentication, payments, permissions or
data-deletion code
Size
Keep pull requests under 400 changed lines where possible; split larger changes
Review turnaround
First response within 1 business day
Author checklist
Tests added, documentation updated, no debug code, linked Jira ticket, screenshots for UI
changes
Merge conditions
All CI checks green, no unresolved comments, branch up to date with target
Merge method
Squash merge into develop; merge commit for release and hotfix branches

Engineering Coding Standards > Page 3

5. Testing
Every feature and bug fix must include automated tests. Minimum line coverage depends on the risk tier of the
module (Figure 2); CI fails when coverage of changed files drops below the tier threshold. Tests must be
deterministic, run without network access to external services, and complete within 10 minutes for the full unit
suite.
Figure 2. Minimum unit-test line coverage by module tier.
For AI and machine-learning code, unit tests cover data validation and pre-processing, and evaluation scripts
run in CI on a fixed sample dataset. Prompt templates and retrieval configurations are stored in version control
and change through pull requests like any other code.
6. Logging, Errors and Observability
• Use structured JSON logs with the fields timestamp, level, service, request_id and message.
• Never log passwords, tokens, API keys or full customer content; mask e-mail addresses and phone
numbers.
• Catch specific exceptions; never use a bare except. Return errors in the API error model.
• Every service exposes /health and /ready endpoints and publishes RED metrics (rate, errors, duration).
7. Security Requirements
• No secrets in code. Credentials are stored in AWS Secrets Manager. Secrets found in a repository must be
rotated immediately and reported to Security within 1 hour.
• Dependency scanning (Dependabot), static analysis (CodeQL) and container scanning (Trivy) run on every
pull request; critical and high findings block the merge.
• Validate and sanitise all external input; use parameterised queries only.
• Use company-approved AI coding assistants only, and never include customer data or credentials in
prompts (see Employee Handbook, Code of Conduct).
8. Documentation
Each repository contains a README.md with purpose, setup, run and test instructions, an owner and an on-call
contact. Public functions use Google-style docstrings. Architecture decisions are recorded as short ADR
documents in /docs/adr.
9. References
